title: Google DeepMind solves 9 Erdős problems
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 21 May 2026 (v1), last revised 8 Jun 2026 (this version, v2)]
Title:Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language models (LLMs) increasingly excel at mathematical reasoning, but their unreliability limits their utility in mathematics research. A mitigation is using LLMs to generate formal proofs in languages like Lean. We perform the first large-scale evaluation of this method's ability to solve open problems. Our most capable agent autonomously resolved 9 of 353 open Erdős problems at the per-problem cost of a few hundred dollars, proved 44/492 OEIS conjectures, and is being deployed in combinatorics, optimization, graph theory, algebraic geometry, and quantum optics research. A basic agent alternating LLM-based generation with Lean-based verification replicated the Erdős successes but proved costlier on the hardest problems. These findings demonstrate the power of AI-aided formal proof search and shed light on the agent designs that enable it.

report.summary: An AI agent combining LLM generation with Lean formal verification autonomously solved 9 open Erdős problems and 44 OEIS conjectures, at a few hundred dollars per problem.
report.background: Large language models have become surprisingly strong at mathematical reasoning, but their tendency to hallucinate makes mathematicians wary of trusting their output. A promising fix is to have models write proofs in formal languages like Lean, where a proof checker gives a binary, un-fakeable verdict. Previous milestones — DeepMind's AlphaGeometry and AlphaProof, which reached IMO silver-medal level in 2024 — showed the approach works on competition-style problems, but it was unclear whether formal proof search could contribute to genuinely open research mathematics. This paper delivers the first large-scale evaluation on open problems, drawing on curated corpora such as the Erdős problems database and OEIS conjectures. Note that while the headline credits Google DeepMind, the arXiv listing is attributed to Swarat Chaudhuri and collaborators, so the institutional framing of the result is worth verifying against the full paper.
key_points: The most capable agent autonomously resolved 9 of 353 open Erdős problems, at a cost of roughly a few hundred dollars per problem — cheap enough that the bottleneck is now verification and significance, not compute.
It also proved 44 of 492 open OEIS conjectures, extending the result from a single famous problem collection to a much broader testbed of combinatorial identities.

Ablations matter: a simpler agent that just alternates LLM generation with Lean verification reproduced the Erdős wins, but burned more money on the hardest problems, suggesting elaborate agent scaffolding buys efficiency rather than new capability.

The system is already being deployed in active collaborations across combinatorics, optimization, graph theory, algebraic geometry, and quantum optics — a sign this is a tooling shift, not just a benchmark result.
The core reliability trick is Lean: every claimed proof is machine-checked, so the AI's known tendency to confabulate cannot silently corrupt the result.
report.impact: For mathematicians, this is the moment AI moves from a cute demo to a co-author-grade collaborator on a small but real subset of open problems. Formal verification gives researchers a trustworthy interface: they can accept a machine result without manually re-deriving it. For the AI industry, it validates a hybrid architecture — neural generation plus symbolic checking — as a general pattern that could extend to chip design, software verification, and scientific discovery. For developers, the demand shifts toward Lean tooling, proof-search orchestration, and agent frameworks rather than raw model scale. For regular users, the immediate effect is indirect but cumulative: faster progress on optimization and combinatorial problems that underpin logistics, scheduling, and cryptography, plus a stronger cultural expectation that AI claims come with machine-checkable receipts.
report.tools: To follow up, start with Lean 4 and its mathlib library, the verification backbone of this work. LeanDojo and the Lean REPL ecosystem let you script proof search; Goedel-Prover and DeepSeek-Prover are open models fine-tuned for Lean proof generation. The Erdős problems database (erdosproblems.com) and OEIS provide the problem pools used here. For newcomers, the Natural Number Game and Mathematics in Lean are the fastest on-ramps to reading machine-checked proofs.
